title: Law-firm catering briefs: meetings, access and dietary notes
body_markdown:
A law firm catering brief is a written plan for feeding colleagues and guests around meetings, with the aim of keeping service organised and interruptions controlled. Specify the meeting format, guest count, building access, dietary requirements and clearance arrangements before requesting proposals. For legal offices, the practical distinction is who can enter the room, when service can happen and what information catering staff actually need.


**TL;DR**

- A law firm catering brief should define meeting times, access permissions, dietary requirements and responsibility for clearing away.
- myCHEF provides corporate event catering; confirm the menu, staffing and practical arrangements in your proposal.
- Choose drop-off catering when your office can manage setup; request staffed service when hosting duties need a named owner.
- Share dietary instructions separately from confidential meeting documents, using meal codes where practical.


## Why a precise catering brief matters for law firms

A working lunch, client presentation and evening reception need different service arrangements. Describe the occasion rather than asking for a generic corporate menu. A lunch delivered during a confidential discussion needs a different handover from refreshments served in an open reception area.

**The brief should tell the caterer how to support the meeting, not explain the legal work.** Keep case details, client documents and discussion notes out of the catering request.

Decide whether your office will receive, arrange and clear the food or whether you want those tasks included in the proposal. The distinction affects what you need to organise internally. If responsibilities are unclear, use the guide to [catering staff and cleanup arrangements](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-catering-companies-in-dubai-provide-serving-staff-and-cleanup) to frame your questions.

## How to write your law firm catering brief

### Define the meeting and service windows

Start with the calendar invitation and write a separate catering schedule. List arrival, setup, food service and collection as distinct moments. A meeting start time does not tell a delivery team when they can unload or enter the room.

For an illustrative 12-person working lunch, distinguish the people eating at the table from anyone joining remotely or arriving after lunch. Do not ask the caterer to infer portions from the full meeting invitation.

Record which timings are fixed and which depend on the chair. If discussions overrun, name the person authorised to release the food for service. Avoid leaving that decision with reception unless reception has accepted the task.

- State the occasion: working lunch, training session, client meeting or reception.
- Give the date, location and number of people eating.
- Separate delivery, setup, service and collection windows.
- Mark periods when the meeting room must remain undisturbed.
- Name the person who can approve a timing change.

### Choose the format before discussing dishes

Use your meeting agenda and room layout to choose a service format manually before comparing menus. Ask whether people can leave their seats, whether a separate food area exists and whether your team can manage replenishment. Those answers narrow the options more effectively than a cuisine preference alone.

Individual meals suit seated working sessions, but distribution and packaging still need an owner. A shared spread gives guests choice, but it needs a suitable surface and a plan for people moving around. Staffed service assigns practical tasks to a team, subject to the agreed scope.

**myCHEF is suited to law firms seeking corporate event catering.** Send the service requirements with your enquiry so the proposal can address the occasion rather than just a list of dishes. Confirm any requested staffing or equipment explicitly; neither follows automatically from the word catering.

- Choose seated meals, a shared spread or staffed service.
- Describe whether guests will eat during a discussion or a break.
- Identify the available serving surface and seating arrangement.
- State who will distribute individual dietary meals.
- Request a clear list of tasks included in the proposal.

### Map access from the loading point to the room

Walk the route with your office or facilities contact. Check where a delivery can stop, which entrance it should use and how food reaches the correct floor. For a Dubai office tower, ask building management about the arrangements that apply to that specific property; do not assume a previous venue's process applies.

Make the destination unambiguous. A building address alone does not identify the reception desk, lift route or meeting suite. Share a delivery contact who can answer during the agreed arrival window.

Keep security instructions practical. Tell the caterer what information building management requests and who will submit it, without circulating confidential guest lists unnecessarily. Any access approval should be confirmed with the building, not inferred from the catering booking.

- Confirm the permitted delivery entrance and unloading point.
- Check whether a loading-bay slot or visitor registration is needed.
- Record the lift route and any trolley restrictions.
- Identify the receiving contact and an internal backup.
- Specify which rooms catering staff may enter.
- Agree where packaging and equipment will wait for collection.

### Match the menu to the room and equipment

Check the facilities yourself before requesting dishes that need finishing, chilling or hot holding. An office pantry is not automatically a preparation kitchen. Describe what is actually present, then ask the caterer to confirm whether the proposed menu works with it.

For a hypothetical 90-minute seated session, consider dishes that guests can eat with the utensils and table space provided. Describe the working conditions: laptops on the table, paper documents nearby or no separate dining area. The caterer can then propose an appropriate menu rather than guessing.

Separate your preferences from confirmed inclusions. Crockery, cutlery, glassware, service utensils and rubbish removal each need an answer. Ask for substitutions to be agreed before service rather than discovered at handover.

- List the available fridge, sink, worktop and power access.
- State whether any cooking or reheating is permitted on site.
- Describe the table space available to each guest.
- Request details of serving equipment and utensils.
- Confirm who supplies drinks, cups and water service.
- Ask how the menu will be handled if the meeting runs late.

### Separate dietary needs from confidential meeting information

Collect dietary requirements directly from attendees through a designated organiser. Ask people to distinguish an allergy from a preference or another dietary requirement. Do not diagnose the requirement yourself or promise that a menu is suitable before the caterer has assessed it.

Use a separate catering sheet rather than forwarding the meeting pack. The operational questions in [catering for law firms](https://blog.gabbeys.com/corporate-event-catering-for-law-firms-complete-guide) concern who eats, where service happens and when access is permitted; they do not require the substance of a client discussion. Share only the information needed to prepare and distribute the meals.

For an illustrative 20-guest seminar, a meal code can connect a dietary portion to its recipient without putting a client name on every label. Agree the coding method with the caterer and keep the organiser's matching list accessible to the person handing out meals.

Ask myCHEF to confirm how the proposed menu addresses the requirements you supply. Do not describe food as allergen-free, halal-certified or suitable for a medical diet unless the relevant claim has been confirmed for that proposal.

- Record allergies separately from preferences and other requirements.
- Ask what ingredient and preparation information can be supplied.
- Agree meal labels and the person responsible for distribution.
- Keep dietary instructions separate from case documents.
- Confirm how late dietary changes will be handled.
- Escalate any unresolved suitability question before approving the menu.

### Confirm responsibilities and approve one final version

Bring the agreed details into a single document and identify its owner. An email trail with different guest counts and menu versions creates avoidable ambiguity. Ask the caterer to acknowledge the final brief and list anything that remains outside scope.

Compare proposals against the same requirements. Guest count, menu complexity, staffing, equipment, access arrangements and service duration are useful questions when discussing the quotation. Ask which elements affect the quoted scope rather than assuming every provider has included the same work.

Finish with the handover and departure arrangements. A room can look cleared while hired equipment, waste or leftovers still need attention. Name the person who signs off the handover and the person who receives any later collection.

- Identify the final brief by date and version.
- Confirm the menu and guest-count approval process.
- Record staffing, equipment and service tasks included.
- List exclusions and responsibilities retained by your office.
- Agree clearing, waste and equipment-collection arrangements.
- Name the contact authorised to approve changes.

## Which catering format fits your meeting?

Choose the format by the work your office can manage, not just the presentation you prefer. These are planning options to discuss in a proposal, not confirmed packages or service inclusions.

| Option | Best for | Main advantage | Key limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individual meals | Seated working lunches | Portions can be assigned to attendees | Distribution and packaging still need managing |
| Shared spread | Breaks with a separate serving area | Guests can choose from the agreed selection | Needs serving space and a clear dietary plan |
| Staffed service | Client hosting where office staff cannot manage food | Service tasks can be assigned explicitly | Staffing, access and duties require agreement |
| Refreshment station | Training sessions with scheduled breaks | Keeps refreshments outside the meeting room | Replenishment and clearing need a named owner |

The decision turns on three practical questions: where food goes, who serves it and who clears it. Answer those before choosing presentation details.

*Choose a format only after assigning space, service and clearing responsibilities.*


## Common mistakes in law-firm catering briefs

### Treating every attendee as a lunch guest

A meeting invitation can include remote participants, organisers and people attending only part of the session. Confirm the number actually eating, then identify any separate requirements for support staff or later arrivals.

### Forwarding the full client agenda

A caterer needs service windows and room-access instructions, not confidential discussion topics. Create a separate operational schedule and keep the client meeting pack within the firm's own process.

### Assuming reception will manage everything

Receiving deliveries, checking labels, setting out food and clearing the room are different tasks. Assign each one explicitly, including cover when reception is busy or away from the desk.

### Approving a menu without checking the pantry

A menu proposal does not confirm that your office has the facilities it needs. Check the actual room, equipment and building permissions before approval, then resolve any mismatch with the caterer.

## FAQ


**What should a law firm catering brief include?**

A law firm catering brief should include the date, location, number eating, service format, access instructions, dietary requirements and clearing responsibilities. Separate delivery and setup times from the meeting start, and name the person authorised to approve changes.

**Is drop-off or staffed catering better for a client meeting?**

Drop-off suits a meeting where your office can manage receiving, setup and clearing; staffed catering suits hosting where those tasks need an assigned service team. Confirm the duties in the proposal rather than assuming staff will handle every task.

**How do we brief a caterer without sharing confidential information?**

Create a separate catering schedule containing only operational details. Share room access, service windows and dietary instructions without forwarding case papers, client discussion notes or the full meeting pack.

**Can a law firm request meals for guests with allergies?**

A law firm can request allergy-specific meals, but suitability must be confirmed with the caterer before approval. Provide the requirements clearly and ask about ingredients, preparation arrangements, labelling and distribution.

**How should we compare catering quotations?**

Compare quotations against the same guest count, menu, service duration, staffing, equipment and clearing requirements. Ask each caterer to identify exclusions so a shorter proposal is not mistaken for an equivalent scope.

**What happens if our meeting runs late?**

Agree the response to an overrun before the event. Name the person who can approve service changes and ask the caterer how delayed service affects the proposed food, staffing and collection arrangements.


## One last check before sending

Ask someone who has not organised the meeting to read the brief. Can they identify the entrance, receiving contact, food destination and clearance owner without asking you? If not, revise the document before requesting a proposal.
